lines: Somebody has been murdered. Six suspects. Six weapons. Nine rooms.
And the answer is sealed in an envelope.
That's three hundred twenty four possible crimes.
Clue was invented in England in the nineteen forties, and it's been sold since nineteen forty nine.
And almost everyone plays it the same way.
They only cross off the cards someone shows them.
But your notepad can do a lot more than that.
So we built Clue in code, and played ten thousand games.
Then we did it again. And again. One for every way of taking notes.
Same cards, same deals. The only thing that changed was the notepad.
We even removed the board, so dice and luck couldn't help anyone.
And the difference is huge. The best note taker solves the case more than twice as fast.
Part one. The basic notepad.
Here's how a turn works. You suggest a suspect, a weapon and a room.
The next player has to show you one of those cards, if they have one.
If they don't, the player after them has to try.
Most people write down that one card, and nothing else.
We gave that player a seat at a four player table.
On average, they needed 10.9 rounds to be sure of the answer.
And in 40 percent of games, it took the full thirteen rounds.
Why so slow? Because one card per turn is the slowest way to search.
At a four player table, there are thirteen or fourteen cards to rule out. You're basically checking them one at a time.
Part two. Watch who passes.
Here's the first upgrade. And it costs nothing.
Every time any player can't show a card, write it down.
That player has none of those three cards. That's three facts, for free.
And it works on other people's turns, too. Not just yours.
With that one habit, the average dropped from 10.9 rounds to 8.1.
Put a basic player and a pass watcher side by side, with the same cards, and the pass watcher finishes first 72 percent of the time.
Part three. Full deduction.
Now the real detective move.
When someone shows a card to another player, you don't see it.
But you still learn something. That player holds at least one of those three cards.
Write it down. Later, when you learn they don't have two of them, the third one is theirs.
And one more trick. Count the cards in each hand.
Once you know all five cards a player has, they can't have anything else. Everything else gets crossed off.
With all three tricks together, here's what happened.
6.5 rounds.
In a head to head race with the same cards, the full deduction player finished first 88 percent of the time.
The basic player won just 4 percent. The rest were ties.
And the fast games got way more common. Solving in five rounds or less went from 6 percent of games to 24.
Part four. Bigger tables.
Now here's the twist. We changed the number of players.
For a basic note taker, more players is bad news.
Three players, 9.9 rounds. Six players, 12.7.
Every round takes longer, and you still learn just one card.
But for the full deduction player, it's the opposite.
Three players, 7.4 rounds. Six players, just 5.4.
More players means more suggestions, more passes, and more hidden cards to track. Every one of them is a clue.
At a six player table, the full deduction player is 2.4 times faster than the basic one.
And in 53 percent of games, they had the answer in five rounds or less.
So how do you win at Clue?
Write down who passes. Write down who showed a card to whom. And count every hand.
Your notepad is the real detective. The dice just move you around.
How do you take notes in Clue? Tell us in the comments.
